a1.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley cited LeadIQ, its AI-powered lead distribution platform, as an early AI use case focused on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with the firm's financial advisors.
items.quote: LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said its ongoing investments in its wealth platform include investments to support its advisors, a build-out of E*TRADE capabilities, and expansion of its workplace channel.
items.quote: Ongoing investments in our world-class platform, including investments to support our advisors, a build-out of E*TRADE capabilities, and the expansion of our essential workplace channel, serve as an engine for future growth.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it put resources toward lending products, including digital tools, digital enhancements and automation to help with the paper backlog associated with lending products.
items.quote: digital tools, digital enhancements and using automation to be able to help with the paper backlog associated with some of the various lending products more broadly.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said the data and insights from its wealth management scale allow its financial advisors (FAs) to tailor advice and equip the firm's tools to deliver that advice.
items.quote: It gives us insights given our size and scale that allow our FAs to tailor advice and equip our own tools to deliver that advice to help clients achieve their goals.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said lending-product household penetration rose through ongoing investments in technology, adviser and client education, and an expanded product set.
items.quote: through ongoing investments in technology, adviser and client education, and an expanded product set.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it continued to invest in deepening its competitive moats in private markets through expanded collaboration with Carta and in digital assets through partnerships with Zero Hash.
items.quote: In the third quarter, we continue to invest, deepening our competitive moats in areas like our expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it is in the early days of the digital asset transformation side of wealth and is looking to expand capabilities through its partnership with Zero Hash.
items.quote: We announced a partnership with Zero Hash last year. We're looking to expand our capabilities. We're well positioned now in the crypto and tokenized asset space.

a1.MS.reason: The passages describe where Morgan Stanley is investing in technology and digital capabilities supporting its advisors and wealth platform.

a2.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Morgan Stanley cites LeadIQ as an AI-powered lead distribution platform focused on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with its financial advisors.
items.quote: LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is working on co-piloting and 'super agents' to drive efficiency and effectiveness across the wealth portfolio.
items.quote: that co-piloting, I think, is something that Jed Finn under the leadership of Andy Saperstein is spending a lot of time on where they effectively have corridors or super agents that are going to be working to drive, again, efficiency and effectiveness across the portfolio in wealth.

items.text: Morgan Stanley says technology it has put in place gives it a greater ability to match advisers to the right clients.
items.quote: we have a greater ability to match advisers to the right clients with all the technology that we've put into place.

items.text: Morgan Stanley says data insights from its size and scale allow its financial advisers to tailor advice and equip its own tools to deliver that advice.
items.quote: It gives us insights given our size and scale that allow our FAs to tailor advice and equip our own tools to deliver that advice to help clients achieve their goals.

a2.MS.reason: The passages describe specific advisor-facing capabilities and tools Morgan Stanley is investing in or deploying.

a3.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley said LeadIQ, its AI-powered lead distribution platform, focuses on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with its financial advisors.
items.quote: LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it is developing co-piloting “super agents” in wealth that use the historical context between a financial adviser and client to drive efficiency and effectiveness across portfolios.
items.quote: And so that co-piloting, I think, is something that Jed Finn under the leadership of Andy Saperstein is spending a lot of time on where they effectively have corridors or super agents that are going to be working to drive, again, efficiency and effectiveness across the portfolio in wealth.

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it is leveraging technology to improve automation and facilitate client acquisition openings, as well as increasing education with its advisors and clients.
items.quote: Growth reflects our efforts to deepen client penetration with SBLs, leveraging technology to improve automation and facilitate the client acquisition openings, as well as increasing education with our advisors and our clients.

a3.MS.reason: Passages state specific AI and automation initiatives connected to financial advisors in Wealth Management.

a4.MS.label: fact

items.text: Management said AI is something that matters to clients and the firm and that the firm is now “double overweight.”
items.quote: I would say that we were overweight and in light of it being something that matters not just to our clients, but to us, I would say we are now double overweight.

items.text: Management said being part of the AI ecosystem and viewed as a trusted adviser—acting as wealth manager, asset allocator and banker—is the firm’s top priority as adviser.
items.quote: we are acting as the wealth manager, the asset allocator, the banker. And for us to be part of the content and the thinking and the evolution of this is absolutely the top priority for the firm as the adviser

items.text: Management said technology is a differentiator in Morgan Stanley’s favor across its self-directed, workplace and financial-adviser platform.
items.quote: And against that platform, we have built a number of advantages that not only allow us to preserve our moat, but actually make technology a differentiator in our favor.

items.text: Management tied world-class technology to supporting clients who want to make decisions with their financial advisers based on their needs.
items.quote: if the technology is world-class, folks want to make decisions with their financial advisers based on the complexity and singularity of their own financial needs

items.text: Management cited LeadIQ, an AI-powered lead distribution platform, as an early AI use case focused on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with financial advisors.
items.quote: LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.

items.text: Management said the firm is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Management highlighted the early stage of digital-asset transformation in wealth, including a Zero Hash partnership and plans to expand crypto and tokenized-asset capabilities and continue work on E*TRADE.
items.quote: I would also call out just the early days of the digital asset transformation side of wealth. We announced a partnership with Zero Hash last year. We’re looking to expand our capabilities. We’re well positioned now in the crypto and tokenized asset space.

items.text: The 10-K said technology supporting evolving client needs, including generative AI and tokenization, is a factor in Wealth Management’s ability to compete across advisor-led, workplace and digital-direct channels.
items.quote: our technology supporting evolving client needs, including generative artificial intelligence and tokenization.

items.text: Management said the scale of the wealth platform supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools.
items.quote: our scale supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools.

a1.MS.label: not_disclosed

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes its Wealth Management clients as individual investors, including high and ultra-high net worth individuals, and businesses and institutions, without naming a mass-affluent segment.
items.quote: Wealth Management provides a comprehensive array of financial services and solutions to individual investors, including high and ultra-high net worth individuals, and businesses and institutions.

a1.MS.reason: The passages describe MS client segments as high and ultra-high net worth individuals and do not use or define a mass-affluent segment.

a2.MS.label: not_disclosed
a2.MS.reason: MS's segment descriptions state Wealth Management serves "individual investors, including high and ultra-high net worth individuals" and small to medium-sized businesses and institutions, but no passage says anything about serving mass-affluent clients and no mass-affluent client metric is reported.

a3.MS.label: different_quantity

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes its Wealth Management funnel as serving 20 million Wealth relationships, with an intense focus on advice generating movement through the funnel to advisor-led assets.
items.quote: With 20 million Wealth relationships, future growth is embedded in the business. Our intense focus on the value of advice, which generates movement through the funnel, allows us to capture opportunities for advisor-led assets.

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes bank-first clients as a top-of-funnel source, saying about one third over time become digital clients or advisor-based clients.
items.quote: those clients that are bank first clients, over time, we've seen that 1/3 of them end up being a digital client or in a relationship and adviser-based client as well... we see a real opportunity to grow the bank, both from a wealth management perspective and the top of the funnel

items.text: Morgan Stanley says it will service clients across all three wealth channels: the financial advisor channel, the everyday transaction offering (E*TRADE), and Workplace, where it partners with companies to reach employees.
items.quote: We're going to service clients across all three channels in wealth: the FA channel, the everyday transaction offering, CashPlus type of offering in E*TRADE. ... we've been really banging the drum on Workplace where we can partner with companies to reach employees.

items.text: Morgan Stanley defines its Core Client Relationships as Advisor-Led Households, Self-Directed Households, and Workplace Participants, excluding overlap.
items.quote: Core Client Relationships represent Advisor-Led Households, Self-Directed Households, and Workplace Participants, excluding overlap, as of 4Q 2020 and 4Q 2025.
items.definition: Core Client Relationships represent Advisor-Led Households, Self-Directed Households, and Workplace Participants, excluding overlap

items.text: A Cerulli Associates report cited in the coverage says 52% of mass-affluent 401(k) participants without an advisor name their retirement savings account provider as their primary source of retirement planning guidance; the passage attributes this to the industry survey, not to Morgan Stanley.
items.quote: A June 2025 Cerulli Associates report found that 63% of active 401(k) participants do not have a financial advisor, while 52% of mass-affluent participants without an advisor say their retirement savings account provider is their primary source of retirement planning guidance.
items.unit: % of mass-affluent 401(k) participants without an advisor

a3.MS.differs_because: No passage has Morgan Stanley describing targeting or attracting 'mass-affluent' clients; the closest material is Morgan Stanley's own descriptions of its broad wealth funnel and channels (advisor-led, self-directed/E*TRADE, Workplace, bank-first clients) and an industry survey statistic about mass-affluent 401(k) participants that is not attributed to Morgan Stanley.

claims.text: Whether each firm names the mass-affluent segment can be compared on this evidence, and Merrill is the most explicit. Merrill (as part of GWIM) explicitly names the segment: in its 2025 investor day materials (November 5, 2025), the 'Wealth Continuum' labels 'Mass Affluent' as clients with $500K–$1MM, alongside 'High Net Worth' of $1MM–$10MM. Schwab refers to 'affluent clients' and 'affluent investors' but does not use the term 'mass affluent'. Morgan Stanley describes its Wealth Management clients as individual investors including high and ultra-high net worth individuals and businesses and institutions, without naming a mass-affluent segment. Edward Jones does not name a mass-affluent segment. Raymond James names high-net-worth, ultra-high-net-worth and 'affluent' clients—higher-wealth tiers than mass-affluent—rather than a mass-affluent segment. The firms are not directly comparable on a single segment definition because only Merrill defines a 'Mass Affluent' band ($500K–$1MM), while Schwab and Raymond James use 'affluent' or higher-net-worth terms without a mass-affluent asset or income definition.

a5.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states that among its initiatives to meet clients' needs is a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones states it has made substantial investments in additional strategies, solutions, products, structures and third-party relationships to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs, including Financial Planning Services offering a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities.
items.quote: The Partnership has been actively pursuing and making substantial investments in additional strategies, solutions, products, structures and third-party relationships (collectively, "initiatives") to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs. These initiatives include both potential future solutions currently in development as well as recently launched products and solutions such as Financial Planning Services, where clients receive a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities.

items.text: Edward Jones states that generational wealth transfer and changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values, may affect its ability to compete and adapt its business model.
items.quote: The Partnership's continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.

items.text: Edward Jones states that its Digital and Data division supports significant investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives to provide new tools for branch teams, and that branch teams leverage new tools for deeper discovery conversations with clients and more comprehensive advice and planning.
items.quote: The Partnership's Digital and Data division supports the significant investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives to provide new tools for branch teams to better serve clients, enhance the operational support the home office provides to the branch teams and create operational efficiencies that reduce manual processes. Branch teams leverage new tools for deeper discovery conversations with clients and more comprehensive advice and planning.

items.text: Edward Jones states that its Enterprise Reimagined initiative will adopt new capabilities, processes and technology to deliver more value and create a better client experience.
items.quote: the firm has embarked on a multi-tiered initiative, called "Enterprise Reimagined," that the firm believes will create more efficient operations by restructuring and reducing the size of the home office, removing redundancies, and adopting new capabilities, processes and technology to deliver more value and create a better client experience.

items.text: Edward Jones announced it took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken with the intention of integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations with clients, and the firm noted it is still determining the deployment strategy.
items.quote: it's notable that this month, Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken , with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

a5.EDJ.reason: Passages state the firm's offerings and initiatives directed at meeting evolving client needs, including a new digital platform aimed at Next Generation investors, without quantifying an alignment measure.

claims.text: Cerulli's 2025 wealth-transfer report (published October 2025) projects that households will transfer $123.7 trillion to heirs and charities between now and 2048.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that of the projected transfer, $105 trillion goes to heirs.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that $18 trillion of the projected transfer goes to charities.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that Generation Xers are expected to inherit $39 trillion.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that Millennials are expected to inherit $46 trillion.

Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that women in the Baby Boomer and older generations are expected to receive $40 trillion in 'horizontal' transfers as they outlive their husbands.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that women in younger generations are expected to receive $47 trillion of the wealth to be transferred intergenerationally.
UBS's 2026 report (published April 2026) estimates that USD 83 trillion in private wealth will change hands globally over the next two to three decades.

Morgan Stanley's 2026 Retirement Plan Survey (trade press, published October 21, 2026) states that as more Americans approach retirement age, employers are under pressure to move beyond compliance-minded plan management toward active participant engagement and personalized financial education.
Schwab's 2Q26 deck (published July 21, 2026) identifies 'the next generations of investors' as one of the forces reshaping its industry.

On the 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said client assets are more concentrated among older generations today, while the average age of its clients continues to get younger.
On the 4Q25 call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab said the average age of its client has fallen by about 10 years in the last decade and is now in the 40s.
On the 4Q25 call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab said a third of its new-to-firm clients last year were Gen Z investors.
Schwab's 3Q26 deck (period ended September 30, 2026) reports that about 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event.
On the 3Q25 call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said nearly one-third of new-to-firm retail households in 2025 were Gen Z investors between ages 13 and 28.
On the 4Q25 call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab said nearly 60% of new retail client accounts opened in 2025 were under age 40.
On the 3Q25 call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab cited industry research that Gen Z is 45% more likely to start investing by age 21 than Millennials.
On the 2Q26 call (period ended June 30, 2026), Schwab said 61% of affluent clients ages 25 to 44 prefer to consolidate their wealth and banking relationships.
Edward Jones' 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025) attributes elevated asset outflows partly to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.

Edward Jones' 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) attributes the continuing downward trend in net new asset outflows in the first nine months of 2025 partly to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.
Edward Jones' 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025) attributes higher asset outflows in the first half of 2025 partly to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.
Edward Jones' 2025 10-K (published March 2026) names generational wealth transfer together with changing client demographics, preferences and values among the strategic risks it seeks to address.
Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states that wealth has been created and concentrated at a rapid pace and is now more likely to be held by older households.
UBS's 2026 report (published April 2026) states the transfer is driven by aging demographics, longer life expectancies and decades of rising asset prices.

Cerulli's 2025 report (published October 2025) states part of the transfer is 'horizontal': women in the Baby Boomer and older generations outlive their husbands and inherit, while women in younger generations receive intergenerational wealth.
UBS's 2026 report (published April 2026) states the next generation coming of age is characterized by global mobility, rapid technological change, and evolving expectations around purpose and impact.

claims.text: On the 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Raymond James said it developed private capital raising expertise and brought in bespoke private investment alternatives for ultra-high-net-worth clients in response to growing demand. Why it might matter: the firm said it is well-positioned to continue investing in its business, people, and technology.

On the 2Q25 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025), CFO Alastair Borthwick said Merrill and the Private Bank continued to add financial advisors through training and experienced hiring, with about one-third of net new households in Q2 added by newly trained advisors. Why it might matter: the CFO said Merrill and the Private Bank added 7,100 net new relationships in the quarter, with the size of relationships continuing to expand.

On the 1Q25 call (period ended March 31, 2025), Schwab said it expected to grow roughly 250 new financial and wealth consultants during 2025 and would continue investing in this in 2026 and 2027. Why it might matter: the firm said relationships are critical to client success and to supporting its 5-7% organic growth rate.

On the 4Q24 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2024), Morgan Stanley said it has an exclusive partnership with Carta, under which Carta will refer private stock plans and corporate companies to Morgan Stanley as they move into going public. Why it might matter: management said the partnership creates opportunities on the wealth side and across the Integrated Firm as those companies move toward going public.

The question of which firm appears most prepared cannot be validly ranked on this evidence because the five firms disclose different, non-comparable measures. Morgan Stanley reports client retention (99%, 2024) and net new assets ($232.4 billion in 3Q26); Schwab reports a wealth-transfer-event retention rate (~75%) and the generational composition of new households (~70% Gen Z/millennials); Edward Jones reports net new assets declines it attributes to generational transfers outside the firm; Merrill reports advisor development and next-generation advisor recognitions (446 advisors on the 2025 Forbes next-gen list) and recruited assets; and Raymond James reports private wealth advisor designations (~450) and intergenerational strategies. These figures use different definitions, units, scopes, and periods, so no same-basis ranking is possible.

claims.text: The client assets per advisor figures across the five firms cannot be validly compared side by side. No firm discloses a client-assets-per-advisor figure, so any such ratio would have to be assembled from each firm's own client-asset and advisor-count measures, which are not on a common basis. Advisor headcounts differ in definition and, for two firms, are not even disclosed: Morgan Stanley labels its count Wealth Management representatives (15,950 at December 31, 2020, a different label and vintage from a 'financial advisors' count); Schwab discloses no advisor headcount, only a total workforce of approximately 33,000 full-time-equivalent employees and ADV regulatory counts of 4,127 employees performing investment advisory functions; Merrill's 18,916 total wealth advisors (December 31, 2023) cover advisors across all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking, not Merrill alone; Edward Jones reports 20,514 financial advisors (June 26, 2026); and Raymond James reports 8,943 employee and independent contractor advisors (September 30, 2025) while excluding RCS-division advisors even though their client assets are included in PCG AUA. The client asset measures likewise differ: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management client assets of $8,433 billion (September 30, 2026), Schwab's firm-wide total client assets, Edward Jones's assets under care of $2.6 trillion, Merrill's client balances, and Raymond James's assets under administration are each defined on a different basis, and Morgan Stanley itself cautions that its non-GAAP measures may be different from or inconsistent with similarly named non-GAAP measures used by other companies.
